questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Visiting Japan has always been a big dream of mine since I love the culture and nature there, so this was an amazing opportunity to really discover the country.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I highly recommend studying abroad, especially in Japan (just don't pick an intense academic program here!)

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy, there were a lot of people hired to help us out, and there were multiple information meetings.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Information meetings once I arrived at the dorm.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: Very easy, but I don't recommend staying at the easy option (Global Village) if you have any other options.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Global Village (which is the dorm for OUSSEP students) is very overpriced and strict with their rules, and I would recommend staying in the city instead or one of the cheaper dorms if possible. Otherwise you could stay at Global Village for 1-2 months to not miss out on the social events, and then find an Airbnb with someone for the remaining time. I found an Airbnb for a month since it was cheaper and the location was much better (middle of Osaka), and I had more freedom.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Be prepared that there is A LOT of paperwork when you arrive and for the first 1-2 months of your stay. Like, a crazy amount. Make sure to go through all of it, preferably with other people to make it a little more bearable. The camera option in Google Translate will be your new best friend (a very difficult-to-understand-best-friend, but essential nonetheless).

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Course registration was fairly easy, but all of the bureaucratic paperwork with the bank, housing, City Hall etc. was a real pain.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There is very helpful English-speaking staff at Global Village that can help you with all of the paperwork, which is why I recommend staying here for the first 2 months.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Very successful, but I know other students were surprised at the limited amount of classes we were allowed to choose, so make sure to familiarize yourself with the OUSSEP curriculum first. Also, a lot of the normal classes that say they are taught in English are actually taught in Japanese, so be careful.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Talk to the other international students or get help from the staff at Global Village or at the IC hall on campus.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was satisfied because I mostly wanted to travel. OUSSEP was academically very easy to follow, so I had a lot of free time.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Most OUSSEP courses are very easy, especially if you choose a topic that you are already familiar with.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: You actually need to show up for class, which was different.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Polymers in Daily Life and Science, Psychology of Perception and Cognition, JA100, Introduction to Scientific English, Independent Study, UC Frontier Science

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Psychology of Perception and Cognition: Very interesting course with a good professor. JA100: I highly recommend studying Japanese since it will make your stay way more enjoyable. But it's a commitment, since it's 3 times a week. Independent Study: Very different course that allows you to study a topic of your own choosing and get insight into Japanese research and work ethic, as well as talk to the locals.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: In total, I think I spent around 100,000 DKK, but I did travel and eat out a lot, and I bought a lot of things. I would suggest having a lot more money than you think you might need, unless you're okay with having to save on a lot of things.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Almost everything was more expensive than I expected. Eating out is affordable compared to Denmark, but cooking your own food is expensive, so you end up eating out 1-2 times a day which means you spend A LOT of money on food (if you want to eat decently well at least). Also, transportation is so expensive. Don't expect European flight prices if you want to travel around the country, and taking the train is just as expensive. Transportation to and from campus is ~30 DKK per day, so it adds up.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I didn't join any clubs since there was already so many social things going on at the dorm with the other international students.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are Japanese clubs that you can join, but I would recommend knowing some Japanese if you want to join those. Otherwise, there are language events and international mingling events as well as some events at the dorm.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I volunteered as an IELTS English tutor for a Japanese student, which I recommend if you get the chance. It was nice to talk to at least one Japanese person since it gives you a lot of insight into the culture, and you might make a new friend.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Travel as much as you can. Japan is an incredible country to travel around, and there are endless things to see and discover. Go to the arcade. Go sing karaoke. Try all of the interesting food. Pray at the temples. Go soak in the onsens. Go have fun in Tokyo. Japan is a giant playground, so make sure to experience as much as you possibly can.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: You just have to always make sure to be very polite to the locals, and they will be very kind to you. I mostly interacted with the international students, so adjusting was easy for me. I think it's difficult if you really have to mingle with the Japanese, since they are usually pretty reserved and not eager to speak English. But most of them are super nice, so it's worth the effort.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Learn Japanese! It's okay if you're not good at it, they will be very happy to see you try, and it might make them more open to speaking English with you. Invite them out to eat, or have a takoyaki party with them.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The Japanese love for bureaucracy and paperwork was exhausting. And towards the end, I was pretty fed up with the politeness since, at times, it becomes almost robotic and not very human. You could also feel that a lot of Japanese people are not very happy with foreigners, especially the older generations.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Funnily enough, also the politeness. Everyone is so kind and helpful and smiling. And everyone takes their time, they're more calm and not in a rush like I'm used to in Denmark. I also loved to spend time at the onsens where you got to see a different side to the locals. Also, Japan is just such a fun place to be, there are endless opportunities for entertainment, so you will never be bored. I also really got to appreciate all of the temples and shrines and the serenity and sacredness of these places. It's a very special atmosphere. I could go on and on about the things I love about Japan, and the positive definitely outweighs the negative.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Travel as much as you can. Don't be afraid to speak Japanese to the locals. Have fun!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Can't think of any.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Becoming friends with the other international students and travelling with them.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I got admitted to a Japanese hospital for 6 days, and no one could speak English there. Another reason why it is so important that you go through all of the paperwork and make sure that you are properly insured. And make friends with someone who speaks Japanese well because you might end up needing them.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
